description: Regulation (EU) 2024/1620 of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing the Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA). Adopted July 2024, operational from 1 July 2025. AMLA is based in Frankfurt. Takes over EBA's AML/CFT mandate and begins direct supervision of highest-risk entities from 2028.

Directive (EU) 2024/1640 on the mechanisms to be put in place by Member States for the prevention of the use of the financial system for money laundering or terrorist financing. Replaces AMLD4 institutional framework. Transposition deadline: 10 July 2026.

New EU supervisory authority established by Regulation 2024/1620. Headquarters in Frankfurt. Operational from 1 July 2025. Takes over direct supervision of the 40 highest-risk financial entities (credit institutions and CASPs) in 2028. Coordinates national supervisors and FIUs.

The main decision-making body of AMLA. Composed of the AMLA Chair and heads of national AML/CFT supervisory authorities from all Member States. Votes on AMLA supervisory decisions, guidelines, opinions, and reports.

AMLA's Executive Board responsible for day-to-day management. Composed of the Chair and five independent members appointed by the Board of Supervisors. Prepares decisions for the Board of Supervisors.

The Chair of AMLA, appointed by the Council of the EU on a proposal from the Commission after open selection procedure. Five-year non-renewable term. Represents AMLA externally and chairs the Board of Supervisors.

Financial entities directly supervised by AMLA from 2028: the 40 highest-risk credit institutions and CASPs operating in at least 6 Member States, selected based on the risk methodology in AMLR. For DSEs, AMLA replaces national supervisor as the lead AML supervisor.

metadata.criteria: operations in ≥6 Member States, highest risk

description: Teams composed of AMLA staff and national supervisory authority staff responsible for day-to-day supervision of Directly Supervised Entities. Modelled on ECB JSTs for banking supervision. AMLA coordinates, national supervisors contribute.

Colleges of supervisors for financial entities with significant cross-border presence but not designated as DSEs. AMLA chairs colleges and ensures convergence. National supervisors retain primary responsibility but AMLA coordinates.

For all non-DSE obliged entities, AMLA exercises indirect supervision: issuing guidelines, opinions, binding technical standards, peer reviews, and supervisory convergence tools. National supervisors retain primary supervisory responsibility.

AMLA hosts and coordinates the network of EU Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs). Takes over the function previously performed by Egmont Group FIU.net at EU level. Facilitates cross-border intelligence sharing and joint FIU analysis.

Central database established by AMLA compiling information from national supervisors and directly supervised entities on AML/CFT risks, beneficial ownership, enforcement actions, and suspicious transaction patterns. Used for supervisory intelligence.

AMLA's tool for assessing the quality and effectiveness of national AML/CFT supervisory authorities. Reviews compare national supervisory approaches against AMLA guidelines and FATF standards. Results published. Binding recommendations where necessary.

AMLA's process for identifying and selecting the 40 Directly Supervised Entities. Based on risk scores derived from: business model risk, geographic presence (≥6 Member States), volume of suspicious transaction reports, supervisory findings, and ML/TF risk indicators.

canonical_name: AMLA RTS on Risk Factors (Art. 29 AMLR)
description: AMLA's mandated Regulatory Technical Standards specifying minimum and higher risk factors that obliged entities must consider in CDD. To replace EBA/GL/2021/02. Expected as final RTS by 2026.

canonical_name: AMLA RTS on CDD Standards (Art. 21 AMLR)
description: AMLA's mandated Regulatory Technical Standards specifying detailed CDD procedures including identification and verification methods, electronic identity verification, and reliance on third parties.

canonical_name: AMLA RTS on Beneficial Ownership Verification
description: AMLA's mandated RTS specifying methods and standards for verifying beneficial ownership information, including use of BO registers and reliability assessments.

canonical_name: AMLA RTS on Group-Level AML/CFT Policies (Art. 15 AMLR)
description: AMLA's mandated RTS specifying requirements for group-wide AML/CFT policies and procedures, information sharing within groups, and treatment of third-country entities.

canonical_name: AMLA RTS on Remote Customer Onboarding
description: AMLA's mandated RTS specifying conditions and requirements for non-face-to-face customer onboarding, including eIDAS-compliant electronic identification methods.

canonical_name: AMLA RTS on EDD for High-Risk Third Countries
description: AMLA's mandated RTS specifying specific EDD measures required for relationships with customers from or transactions linked to high-risk third countries identified by the EU Commission.
AMLA's mandated Implementing Technical Standards specifying common supervisory methodology for national AML/CFT supervisors, including risk-based supervisory scoring and inspection approaches.

canonical_name: AMLA ITS on AML/CFT Database Reporting
description: AMLA's mandated ITS specifying data formats and requirements for national supervisors and DSEs to report AML/CFT data to the AMLA central database.

AMLD6 harmonises the list of predicate offences for money laundering across Member States, requiring criminalisation of all 22 FATF-listed predicate offences including cybercrime, environmental crime, and tax crimes.

AMLD6 requires Member States to impose minimum criminal sanctions for ML offences: minimum 4 years imprisonment for natural persons, and effective corporate liability with fines up to 10% of global annual turnover for legal persons.

AMLD6 requires Member States to maintain interconnected BO registers (trusts, companies). BO registers must be interconnected via the BRIS system (Business Register Interconnection System) and accessible to competent authorities, obliged entities, and the public (with appropriate access levels).

AMLD6 (2024/1640) replaces and supersedes AMLD4 (2015/849) as the primary AML directive governing national institutional frameworks. AMLD5 crypto provisions now absorbed into AMLR. AMLD6 focuses on institutional structure, national supervisor powers, and criminal law.

AMLA's process for developing RTS and ITS: (1) AMLA develops draft; (2) Public consultation period (typically 3 months); (3) AMLA publishes final draft; (4) European Commission endorses and publishes in Official Journal. AMLA must publish 30+ mandated standards.

AMLA issues non-binding guidelines and opinions on the application of AMLR and AMLA Regulation provisions. These supplement binding RTS/ITS. National supervisors must comply or explain. Replaces EBA's AML guideline function from 2025.

AMLA (Regulation 2024/1620) establishes the institutional framework for supervising compliance with AMLR (Regulation 2024/1624). The two regulations are complementary: AMLR sets substantive obligations; AMLA provides the supervisory architecture to enforce them.

AMLA takes over EBA's AML/CFT mandate from 1 July 2025: guideline issuance, supervisory convergence, FIU coordination, and the role of lead supervisor for cross-border institutions. EBA retains prudential supervision role. Ongoing EBA AML guidelines remain valid until replaced by AMLA standards.

AMLA's supervisory methodology and standards are designed to align with FATF Recommendations, particularly R.26 (Regulation and Supervision) and R.27 (Powers of Supervisors). AMLA's peer review mechanism mirrors FATF mutual evaluation process.

Member States must transpose AMLD6 by 10 July 2026. Key transposition requirements: expanded predicate offences, criminal sanctions harmonisation, BO register interconnection, enhanced national supervisor powers (inspection, sanction), FIU information sharing powers.

AMLA's supervisory powers over Directly Supervised Entities: on-site inspections, off-site reviews, binding decisions, fines (up to 10% of annual turnover or €10M for serious breaches), periodic penalty payments, and public statements.

AMLD6 requires Member States to grant national AML supervisors enhanced powers: right to inspect any obliged entity, access all relevant data, impose administrative fines, issue binding decisions, and publish enforcement decisions. Minimum fine levels harmonised.

AMLA coordinates the network of national FIUs within the EU. Facilitates: joint analysis, spontaneous information exchange, cross-border case coordination, common metrics, and annual FIU report. Replaces informal FIU.net coordination.

AMLD6 requires each Member State to designate national competent authorities (NCAs) with responsibility for AML/CFT supervision of financial and non-financial obliged entities. NCAs must be adequately resourced and independent.

AMLD6 encourages Member States to designate a single AML/CFT supervisor for the financial sector (or clearly delineate responsibilities if multiple supervisors exist). Prevents supervisory gaps and arbitrage between supervisors.
